text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementPsychologyIs Science a Mirror, a Game, or a Conversation?What separates science from non-science KFBy Kristen French1:00 PM CST on November 16, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleScience is a slippery concept. It’s tough to fit into a neat box with fixed edges. It is digging up artifacts in the desert, peering at microbes through powerful instruments, theorizing about the expansion of the universe, writing code for new technology, retracting a paper riddled with errors, admitting you were wrong, starting over, making accidental discoveries, experimenting on yourself with psychedelic drugs. It is also exploring genetic code, curing disease, connecting people through instant global communication, and engineering weapons of mass destruction. It is demystifying rainbows. It is riddled with bias, but it is the most rigorous system humans have for discovering things about the world.But what separates science from non-science exactly and who decides? Recently, University of California, Berkeley, psychologist Marina Dubova and Princeton University researcher Qiawen E. Liu decided to try to take on the elusive task of answering these questions—of defining science.Read more: “The Thrill of Science in 2042”Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
